Paragraph: I rushed towards the sound and to my dismay beheld a young ascetic, whose body was covered with blood and dust. A broken pot lay by his side bearing mute witness to my sin. As I stood quivering with fear he looked at me like one who wanted to immolate me in the blaze of his anger.'Speaking harshly he said, 'To fetch a pot of water for my parents I had come here, but now that I am struck, my parents too will perish.' He then asked me to quickly take some water to his old parents but warned me to pacify his father first, so as to avert any curses he may pronounce. He also asked me to remove the arrow still in his body, as the pain was unbearable. I stood rooted to the ground, miserable and horrified. Beholding my sorrow, he said gently, 'My mind grows peaceful. I no longer grieve and I will soon be dead. And you, king will not be guilty of killing a Brahmin, for I am no Brahmin, but born of a 'Sudra' mother and a Vaisya' father'. I then pulled out the arrow and he shuddered with pain, until death released him from his suffering. An innocent life was lost and I was to blame. Though unwitting it was still a sin irreversible and unpardonable.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dasaratha recounts the traumatic experience of discovering he had accidentally killed an ascetic, whose dying words convey immense concern for his blind parents. Dasaratha is paralyzed by fear, misery, and horror, unable to act effectively. The ascetic's instructions highlight the dire consequences of Dasaratha's action for his elderly, dependent parents.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: The passage portrays the immediate and overwhelming impact of causing unintended harm. Dasaratha's psychological state is one of extreme distress, marked by physical incapacitation ('rooted to the ground'). The ascetic's initial anger and subsequent peaceful acceptance, along with his clarification about his caste, provide a complex emotional and moral landscape for Dasaratha's guilt. Despite the ascetic's reassurance about the Brahmin aspect, Dasaratha still internalizes the act as an 'unpardonable sin,' emphasizing the deeply personal nature of his culpability.
Outcome/Resolution: The ascetic dies, released from his suffering, but Dasaratha is left with the indelible burden of having taken 'an innocent life' and committed an 'irreversible and unpardonable sin.' His profound guilt and self-blame are cemented, leading to lasting psychological torment that eventually manifests in his present-day suffering.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Karma Phala (The consequence of the 'unwitting' sin, which Dasaratha explicitly states is 'irreversible and unpardonable.')
Papa (The 'sin' of taking an innocent life, regardless of intent, leading to profound spiritual and psychological burden.)
Dukha (The suffering experienced by Dasaratha ('miserable and horrified') and the ascetic, whose initial pain is followed by a peaceful surrender to death.)
Krodha (The ascetic's initial 'blaze of anger,' which he later transcends to a state of peace.)
Moha (The initial delusion or mistaken perception that led to the act, the seed of the Karma.)
Mumukshutva (The ascetic's desire for liberation from suffering, as 'death released him from his suffering,' illustrating a spiritual release.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage details Dasaratha's confrontation with the immediate and profound 'Papa' (sin) of taking an innocent life, emphasizing the Karma Phala of even an unwitting act. His emotional paralysis and overwhelming guilt upon witnessing the ascetic's death highlight the devastating spiritual consequences. The ascetic's journey from 'Krodha' (anger) to a peaceful transcendence of 'Dukha' (suffering) offers a counterpoint to Dasaratha's lingering spiritual burden. Despite the ascetic's clarification of his caste, Dasaratha internalizes the act as an 'unpardonable' breach of spiritual law.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this passage is an intense depiction of acute trauma and the immediate onset of profound guilt and self-blame. Dasaratha is paralyzed by fear and shock upon realizing his fatal error, experiencing intense misery and horror. The ascetic's dying words, revealing the devastating impact on his parents, deeply ingrain in Dasaratha the irreversible nature of his 'unpardonable sin,' leading to a lasting burden of culpability. His description highlights the profound emotional distress and internal suffering that follows such a traumatic, accidental but devastating act.
